title: India's Opposition Alliance Is Breaking Apart. The DMK Just Refused to Show Up.
excerpt: The INDIA bloc's biggest southern ally says Congress committed a 'betrayal' in Tamil Nadu. With both the DMK and AAP sitting out the June 8 meeting, the opposition front is more fragmented than at any point since its founding.
body:
The Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance — the INDIA bloc — is heading into what should be its most important strategy session since the 2024 general elections. Instead, it is heading into it without two of its most powerful members.

The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam on Thursday announced it will not attend the June 8 meeting of the opposition alliance in New Delhi. The party, which governs Tamil Nadu and commands 22 Lok Sabha seats, said the decision reflected the "deep hurt" felt by its cadre over what it called a betrayal by the Indian National Congress.

The Tamil Nadu Fault Line

The rupture traces back to the recent Tamil Nadu Assembly elections. The DMK and Congress had fought together as allies — a partnership that stretched back decades and delivered Congress five seats in the state legislature. But when the results came in, Congress chose to abandon that alliance. It threw its support behind Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam, the new political party led by actor-turned-politician C. Joseph Vijay, helping TVK cross the majority threshold and form the government.

For the DMK, this was not a routine political realignment. It was a betrayal of a foundational alliance. Udhayanidhi Stalin, the DMK leader and son of party president M.K. Stalin, accused Congress of choosing political expediency over loyalty. DMK MP Kanimozhi took the unusual step of requesting the Lok Sabha Speaker to reassign seating for DMK lawmakers — a symbolic severing of ties within the parliamentary chamber itself.

"In view of the sentiments of DMK cadres, who continue to feel deeply hurt by what they consider the betrayal committed by the Congress party against the DMK following the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly elections, and in respect of those sentiments, the DMK will not participate in the INDIA alliance meeting," the party said in a statement.

A Bloc With Widening Gaps

The DMK's absence compounds existing fractures. The Aam Aadmi Party has already publicly distanced itself from the bloc and is not expected to attend. The Trinamool Congress, while likely to send a delegation led by Mamata Banerjee and Abhishek Banerjee, is nursing its own grievances — internal dissent from MLAs who have defied the party leadership in West Bengal.

What remains is a coalition meeting at the Constitution Club with roughly 15 parties, headlined by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Rahul Gandhi, Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Uddhav Thackeray, and Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav. They will discuss strategy for upcoming state elections, particularly Uttar Pradesh, and attempt to project unity against the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance.

But the optics are difficult to ignore. The INDIA bloc was conceived in June 2023 as a unified counter to the BJP's dominance. Its last formal meeting was in June 2024, ahead of the general elections, where it managed to deny the BJP a standalone majority. Since then, the alliance has held together more on paper than in practice.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, the fragmentation of the opposition carries implications beyond domestic politics. A weakened opposition means less legislative resistance to policies that affect NRIs — from tax treaties to dual citizenship proposals to consular services reform. The INDIA bloc's ability to function as a coherent check on the ruling dispensation is directly proportional to how many of its members are willing to sit in the same room.

The DMK was careful to note that while it would skip this meeting, it would "continue, as always, to raise its voice on issues affecting the welfare of the nation." But a voice raised from outside the room carries less weight than one raised within it.

What Comes Next

The June 8 meeting will proceed, but it will do so as a diminished exercise. Congress, the bloc's anchor party, faces the uncomfortable reality that its Tamil Nadu gambit — backing Vijay's TVK — has cost it one of its most reliable allies without guaranteeing any new ones. The question now is whether this is a temporary rift that skilled backroom diplomacy can heal, or whether the INDIA bloc has entered a phase of irreversible decline.

The last time India's opposition fragmented this badly was in the early 2010s, when multiple regional parties drifted away from the United Progressive Alliance. That fragmentation gave the BJP its first full majority in 2014. History, it seems, is testing whether it will repeat itself.
